newsitem.title: USA: Yahoo sees further strong page view growth.
newsitem.headline: Yahoo sees further strong page view growth.

text.p: Senior executives of the leading Internet navigation and media company Yahoo! Inc said the company is experiencing continued strong growth in Web traffic so far this year.

We've seen very strong growth in page views in January and in February, Gary Valenzuela, Yahoo! senior vice president of finance and chief financial officer, told investors at a technology conference here.

Page views provide an indication of the traffic on Yahoo's Web site. In the month of December, Yahoo! reported it was averaging 20 million page views a day, as many as its three principle rivals combined.
This was up from 15 million a day in September and from just four million in the month of December 1995.

In a presentation to the Robertson Stephens & Co conference, Valenzuela told investors the company investors that despite some prospect of seasonal sluggishness in the advertising market early in the year, 1997 revenues should jump on a year-on-year basis.
"Clearly the opportunity is for very strong year over year revenue growth in each quarter of 1997," he said.
"The key point is that we've been close to profitability in each quarter," Valenzuela said.
"The key message I believe, as you look at the competitors, is you don't want to stray too far from profitability because it is difficult to find your way back," he added.
Three Internet navigation competitors -- Excite Inc, Lycos Inc and Infoseek -- also raised money in initial public offerings last spring.
"We only used $3 million of cash in all of 1996," said Valenzuela, adding that competitors typically have a quarterly cash outflow of at least that level.

"In our case, barter revenues are, have been and will be immaterial, so less than five percent of our Q4 revenues came from barter," he said. "These are real revenues coming from all advertising customers."
Analysts have raised concerns that at least one rival of Yahoo! had been reporting a higher level of barter.

The CFO also noted that seasonality of revenues is very normal in the advertising business, drawing parallels to traditional media companies. "Strong Q4s are usually followed by weak or flattish Q1s," he said.
Valenzuela said it may take another year or more of operations for the company, which just went public in April 1996, to understand the roll of seasonality in its revenue stream.

Robertson Stephens analyst Keith Benjamin, for example, expects Yahoo! revenues to slip sequentially in the first quarter to $8.3 million from $8.6 million in fourth quarter 1996, but this would be well above the $1.7 million it reported in the year-ago quarter.
Total Yahoo! revenues could jump to $43.8 million in 1997 from $19.1 million last year, according to Benjamin.

Valenzuela said analysts have estimated Yahoo! only sold around 25 percent of its available advertising page spaces in its recent quarter, adding 90 percent is probably realistic at some point in the future.
Valenzuela said the company's $102 million in cash at year-end 1996 provided the company with the financial reserves to grow both internally and through external resources.
Yahoo! President and CEO Timothy Koogle said the company has already signed up 500,000 users of its customized My Yahoo pages in the first two months it was available at the end of last year.
